title: Rational curves of higher degree on U_n/ℚ(n) with floor/sqrt: 'Puiseux identities'
connection: Mordell–Schinzel kills polynomial identities (rational curves over ℚ(n)) on square classes. But identities over ℚ(√n) (i.e. n = m² and x,y,z polynomials in m) are allowed and exist (the m² case has solutions from m). The question for primes: identities over ℚ(n^{1/k}) are not applicable since p is not a k-th power — but identities over ℚ(√(n+a)) could apply when n+a is a square. A 'union over a' cover? Each a covers a sparse set (n = m² − a), total density 0 — so no, unless a varies with n. Record and drop? Keep as an item: 'Schinzel's theorem for algebraic-function identities'.
why: Clarifies what algebraic-function identities can and cannot do; Schinzel may have covered it.
first_step: Search 'Schinzel identities Erdős–Straus algebraic function of n'; read Schinzel 2000 'On sums of three unit fractions with polynomial denominators'.
alt_first_steps: [upgrades-0276] Search polynomial X, Y, Z of degree ≤ 4 in m for k = 1, 2, 3, 5, 7 (with congruence conditions on m), via undetermined coefficients.

title: Ergodic Ramsey: Furstenberg correspondence for the set of (C, a) certificates as a subset of ℕ² with positive density
connection: The set W = {(C, a) : a ≡ −1 mod 4C} has density 0 in ℕ² but positive 'logarithmic' density along C; ES says the map p ↦ (p mod a) hits a prescribed class in W for every p. Furstenberg's correspondence turns density into recurrence; multiple recurrence (Szemerédi-type) gives patterns in every positive-density set but says nothing about one specific p.
why: Probably a dead end, but 'ES for all p' resembles 'recurrence for every point' = topological dynamics (minimal systems), where pointwise results (Birkhoff, Hindman) exist. Is the ES certificate set a return-time set of a minimal system?
first_step: Formulate: R = {n : n has a certificate}; is R an IP-set or a thick/syndetic set? (Trivially syndetic since n ≡ 2,3 mod 4 always work.) Refine to primes: is the set of 'good C' syndetic in C for each fixed p? Check numerically whether gaps between winning C are bounded for fixed p.

title: Type I with d = 1 only: the 'sum of two squares' subfamily of ES
connection: Setting d = 1 in Type I gives p² + (2c)² = f·g with f ≡ −p (mod 4c). Since p ≡ 1 mod 4, p = u² + v² (Fermat); p² + 4c² = (p + 2ci)(p − 2ci) in ℤ[i] — f corresponds to an ideal divisor of (p + 2ci). The Gaussian integer structure is fully explicit: f = N(α) for α | p + 2ci. The congruence f ≡ −p mod 4c is then a condition on α mod 4c in ℤ[i].
why: This subfamily lives entirely in ℤ[i], where everything is computable via Gaussian factorisation; a complete analysis (which p have a d=1 Type I solution? density? structure of failures?) is a clean sub-problem; failures are the input to the general problem.
first_step: Compute the set of p ≤ 10⁷ with no d=1 Type I solution for c ≤ 10⁴; density, structure (do they correlate with p's Gaussian factorisation u + vi?).

title: Lens space L(p,A) not homotopy-equivalent to L(p,1), bounding a 3-chain plumbing
connection: p/A = [[v,t,u]] means L(p,A) bounds the linear plumbing with Euler numbers −v,−t,−u. Whitehead: L(p,q) ≃ L(p,q′) iff qq′ ≡ ±m² (mod p). For p ≡ 1 (4) prime, (A/p) = −1 ⇔ L(p,A) ≄ L(p,1). So ES₅(p) ⇔ some lens space of order p that is not homotopy-equivalent to L(p,1) bounds a negative-definite linear plumbing with 3 vertices.
why: Turns ES₅ into a 3-manifold statement about the 'plumbing length' of homotopy types, where the homotopy type is the ES sign.
first_step: Tabulate min plumbing length over the non-L(p,1) homotopy class for p < 10⁵ (= λ(p)); look for 4-manifold invariants (d-invariants, Casson–Walker) that bound plumbing length from above.

title: Gross–Zagier / Waldspurger: the count of certificates as a toric period, nonvanishing ⟺ L(1/2) ≠ 0
connection: If the certificate count is a sum of a theta-type function over a torus orbit (CM points), Waldspurger's formula expresses |sum|² as L(1/2, f × χ) — nonvanishing of L-values implies nonvanishing of the count. Non-vanishing of L(1/2) for *every* twist in a family is open in general, but for specific families (e.g. by Goldfeld's conjecture) it holds for 'most'.
why: Converts ES-like positivity into L-value nonvanishing — a well-studied (if hard) target with GRH-conditional results (one nonvanishing twist among polylog many). Need the dictionary.
first_step: Formulate: is Σ_{d | 4Cp+1} χ(d) (χ of order 2 mod 4C with χ(−1) = −1) a toric period of an Eisenstein series? (Eisenstein, not cuspidal — then Waldspurger is replaced by Hecke's formula for L(s, χ)L(s, χ') — which is explicit!) Compute: the twisted divisor sum Σ_{d|N} χ(d) = coefficient of E(χ,1); positivity of this coefficient at N = 4Cp+1 is the question; it factors over primes q | N as Π (1 + χ(q) + … ); it's zero iff some prime q ∥ N has χ(q) = −1 … so the sign structure is completely explicit per C. Document.
alt_first_steps: [tools-0170] Check whether the class-group character expansion of the Type I count has nonnegative coefficients so that Waldspurger applies termwise.
refs: Waldspurger, Sur les valeurs de certaines fonctions L automorphes en leur centre de symétrie, Compositio 54 (1985)

title: Probability: Lovász Local Lemma for 'p avoids all classes' — dependency graph of the events across (C, a)
connection: LLL gives existence of an outcome avoiding all 'bad' events when each has small probability and few dependencies; here we want the OPPOSITE (no p avoids all good events), i.e. LLL would be used to show a counterexample is *consistent* — a disproof-side consistency check. Compute the dependency structure: events E_{C,a} = {p ≡ r mod a} for different a are dependent only via CRT (independent for coprime moduli!).
why: Since residues mod coprime moduli are 'independent' in the CRT sense, the LLL/CRT construction shows there exist INTEGERS avoiding any finite collection of classes (as long as the classes don't cover) — but primality is the constraint that breaks the construction; so a counterexample must exist as an integer for each finite K (trivial: odd squares!) and ES hinges on primality + infinitely many K. Record precisely as a 'what the problem is' statement.
first_step: Note that odd squares are integers avoiding ALL classes (T1); so the integer version of 'avoid all' has solutions; ES is about primes. Write up the distinction and the role of primality in the C-form: p prime enters only via... nothing?! The C-form condition 4Cp+1 = ab makes no use of p's primality — so the C-form conjecture 'every non-square n has a C-form certificate' is the right integer statement, and its exceptions (409, 577, 5569, 9601 among primes; plus composites?) are the data.

title: Artin's primitive-root conjecture (Hooley, GRH) as the model for 'a fixed p with a property across infinitely many moduli'
connection: Hooley proves (on GRH) that a fixed a is a primitive root mod infinitely many primes q — a statement about ONE integer a across a family of moduli, via Chebotarev in Kummer fields ℚ(ζ_k, a^{1/k}) + GRH error control. ES: one prime p must have 'a good residue' (a certificate) mod some 4cd, across the family — same shape ('fixed base, varying modulus')! Hooley's method is pointwise in a.
why: This is the closest known shape to ES among proved (conditional) theorems: fixed element, varying field family, existence (indeed density) of good moduli — and it is PROVED (GRH). The repo's survey may have missed it. The key: Artin needs infinitely many good q and gets density; ES needs ONE good (c,d), which is weaker.

Then check whether Hooley's GRH-conditional machinery (effective Chebotarev in ℚ(ζ_k, ·)) gives: for a positive proportion of c ≤ X, the certificate exists — i.e. f(p) → ∞ on GRH?! title: Cyclotomic rigidity directly: primes dividing Φ_m(x) are ≡ 1 mod m (or divide m). Find x, m with Φ_m(x) = 4Cp+1 and m | ... so that divisors ≡ 1 mod m; need ≡ −1 mod 4C though — use Φ_{2m} or the factor structure of x^m + 1
connection: Prime divisors q of x^m + 1 (odd m) satisfy q ≡ 1 mod 2m or q | 2(x+1)... more precisely primitive divisors of x^{2m} − 1 are ≡ 1 mod 2m. To get divisors ≡ −1 mod 4C we need a different rigidity: primes dividing x² + 1 are ≡ 1 mod 4 (wrong sign); primes dividing x² − 2 are ≡ ±1 mod 8; primes dividing x² + 2 are ≡ 1, 3 mod 8 — the '3 mod 8' is ≡ −1 mod 4 but not −1 mod 8. In general, primes dividing a binary form of discriminant D lie in classes determined by (D/q) = 1 — a *set* of classes, never a single class −1 mod 4C unless the genus theory is trivial. So cyclotomic/quadratic-form rigidity gives 'divisors in a SUBGROUP', not in a coset — and −1 mod 4C must be IN that subgroup. For 4C = 8: the subgroup {1,3} mod 8 (from x² + 2) contains 3 ≢ −1; {1,7} (from x² − 2) contains 7 ≡ −1 ✓. So: if 4Cp + 1 = x² − 2 for some x, then every prime factor is ≡ ±1 mod 8, and the product... need a divisor ≡ 7 mod 8 — exists iff some prime factor is ≡ 7 mod 8 (else all ≡ 1). Not forced. Conclusion: quadratic-form rigidity gives subgroup membership, not coset hitting. Record as a structured negative with the one escape: forms whose 'divisor subgroup' is exactly {±1} mod 4C make the problem a parity question.
why: Pinning down that classical rigidity (cyclotomic/quadratic) gives subgroups not cosets, and identifying the parity escape, is a reusable lemma for the 'generator matrix'.
first_step: Write the lemma; then search for binary forms Q with divisor subgroup {±1} ⊂ (ℤ/4C)^× for small C (requires (ℤ/4C)^× to have a large... only C = 1 or 2 work, since index must be φ(4C)/2 for a quadratic form's genus… no: the subgroup of 'split primes' for ℚ(√D) has index 2; {±1} has index φ(4C)/2; equal only if φ(4C) = 4, i.e. 4C ∈ {8, 12}: C = 2, 3). So for C = 2: x² − 2 (divisors ≡ ±1 mod 8); C = 3: x² + 3 (divisors ≡ 1 mod 3 — hmm need ±1 mod 12: primes dividing x² + 3 are ≡ 1 mod 3 i.e. ≡ 1, 7 mod 12 — wrong). Tabulate properly.

title: Mechanism design: an identity family indexed by the Gaussian factorisation p = u² + v² (not polynomial in p but polynomial in (u, v))
connection: Mordell–Schinzel forbids polynomial identities in p on square classes; identities polynomial in (u, v) with p = u² + v² are a different class (p is a quadratic form in the parameters). E.g. try: 4/(u² + v²) = 1/x(u,v) + 1/y(u,v) + 1/z(u,v) with x, y, z ∈ ℤ[u, v] — a polynomial identity in TWO variables over the quadric. Schinzel's theorem is about one variable n; a two-variable identity covering all (u, v) with u² + v² ≡ 1 mod 24 is not obviously excluded (but a polynomial identity in (u,v) specialises to a polynomial identity in n on... no — n = u² + v² does not make x(u,v) a polynomial in n). Also allowed: identities depending on (u, v) mod small moduli.
why: A genuinely different identity class that respects T1 automatically? (Odd squares m² = u² + v² with... m² = (m)² + 0² or other representations; identities valid only for v ≠ 0 or for gcd(u,v) = 1 would exclude the trivial representation — promising sign.) Search space is small; cheap to run.
first_step: For hard primes ≤ 10⁷ compute (a,b) and fit low-degree polynomial forms to the smallest solutions' denominators; check B1 Thm M's scope for procedures that use the two-squares decomposition.

title: Convolution-on-group view: the divisor multiset of N mod 4C is a multiset D ⊂ (ℤ/4C)^×; certificates = D ∋ −1; D = product-set of the prime-power 'intervals' {1, q, …, q^e} — a Minkowski product of 'geometric progressions' in the group; Kneser's theorem bounds |D| from below
connection: |D| ≥ Σ (|D_q| − 1) + 1 (Cauchy–Davenport analogue for abelian groups via Kneser) when there is no stabiliser; so with ω(N) factors, |D| ≥ ω + 1 roughly — tiny versus φ(4C). Kneser's theorem also says: if |D| is small then D is a union of cosets of a subgroup H (periodic) — then −1 ∈ D iff the coset structure includes it: a *structural* dichotomy: either D is large (random-like, then −1 ∈ D with 'probability' |D|/φ) or D is periodic with stabiliser H (then −1 ∈ D ⟺ −1 ∈ D·H, a subgroup question). This is a rigorous version of the 'subgroup vs subset-product' gap.
why: Kneser's structure theorem is a real theorem applicable pointwise (at each (p, C)); it reorganises failures into 'small non-periodic D' (few factors — the dominant failure mode) vs 'periodic D missing −1' (subgroup obstruction).
first_step: For (p, C) failures, compute D, its stabiliser H = {h : hD = D}, and classify; check the Kneser bound tightness.
alt_first_steps: [tools-0268] Apply Kneser iteratively to the divisor sets of consecutive slices pooled in one group (common e) and record stabiliser chains.
[upgrades-0128] For hard primes and C ≤ 100 compute |product set|/φ(4C) and the Kneser stabiliser; classify failures.

title: Cubic surface 4xyz = nw(xy+yz+zx) as a Cayley-type nodal cubic: Heath-Brown's Cayley cubic counting
connection: The projective closure is a singular cubic surface. Its singularity type (nodes) places it near Cayley's cubic, whose rational point count was computed by Heath-Brown and de la Bretèche via torsor parametrisations.
why: Universal torsors linearise rational points on singular cubics. An integral-point analogue (torsors over the log pair) could parametrise ES solutions by lattice points in a region.
first_step: Determine the singularity type of the closure (via sympy). If it is a 4A₁ Cayley cubic, write its universal torsor and the integral-points condition in torsor coordinates.

title: Ellenberg–Michel–Venkatesh: Linnik's ergodic method with a split-prime condition
connection: EMV prove equidistribution of integer points on spheres (and representations of lattices) assuming a fixed prime splits — Linnik's condition; ES-related ternary representations have exactly this kind of auxiliary prime condition.
why: Linnik's method gives results at individual large integers, not on average — the pointwise shape ES needs — at the cost of a splitting condition.
